output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is severely impaired: RAVLT delayed recall at the 1st percentile and immediate recall at the 3rd percentile, consistent with a storage-type encoding deficit; cuing does not improve performance. Visuospatial memory is also markedly impaired (Rey Complex Figure Delayed Recall, 5th percentile) despite preserved copy (25th percentile). Semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile) are significantly below expected norms. Letter fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile) and executive set-shifting (Trail Making B, 15th percentile) are mildly reduced. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 28th percentile) is within low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 17/30. Mood screening is normal (GDS 3/15). Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, multi-domain type

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

Consider the single case-designated optional biomarker route if biological confirmation would change management or uncertainty remains when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

key_clinical_evidence: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the reviewed cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Biomarker route: optional CSF Alzheimer biomarkers, with no duplicate CSF/PET confirmation.
key_educational_points: Early AD typically presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Vascular risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension are modifiable contributors to cognitive decline and should be optimized
APOE genotype is a risk modifier and is not a diagnostic test for Alzheimer disease
CSF biomarkers (Abeta42, phospho-tau, total tau) provide in vivo confirmation of Alzheimer pathology
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate AD
Mixed AD and vascular pathology is common and does not preclude an AD diagnosis when the amnestic phenotype predominates
This case exposes optional CSF Alzheimer biomarkers as its only biomarker route; conclusive CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET must not be ordered together

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Takeshi Yamamoto is a 81-year-old right-handed retired postal carrier who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Doris, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past two years. His wife reports that she first noticed changes roughly two years ago when he began misplacing his keys and wallet with increasing frequency, which she initially attributed to normal aging. However, over the past twelve months the problems have become substantially worse and harder to dismiss. He now frequently forgets conversations they had earlier the same day and asks the same questions repeatedly, sometimes three or four times in a single afternoon. He has been an avid fisherman for decades but last summer left his tackle box at the lake on two separate occasions and once drove to a different boat launch than the one he had used for thirty years, becoming confused about which road to take. His wife reports that she discovered unpaid utility bills stuffed in a desk drawer three months ago; he had always handled the household finances meticulously and this was deeply out of character. She has since taken over bill paying and checkbook management. He missed two follow-up appointments with his primary care physician despite having them written on the kitchen calendar, apparently forgetting to check it. At their church, where he has been a deacon for twenty years, fellow members have remarked that he seems quieter than usual and occasionally loses his train of thought during conversations. His wife also notes that he tried to assemble a new bookshelf from a kit two months ago, a task that would have been straightforward for him previously, but became frustrated and confused by the instructions and eventually gave up. He continues to dress, bathe, and feed himself independently, though his wife has begun laying out his clothes because he sometimes picks out mismatched outfits. He still drives locally on familiar routes but his wife no longer feels comfortable with him driving at night or in unfamiliar areas. He denies any hallucinations, personality changes, or aggressive behavior. He has no history of falls, seizures, focal weakness, or tremor. His sleep pattern is unchanged and his wife denies witnessing any acting out of dreams. His appetite is fair, and he has lost approximately five pounds over the past six months without trying. He appears somewhat subdued during the interview and occasionally looks to his wife for confirmation of details but does not appear overtly depressed.
